A supervision failure and the shutdown of the Launch Manager
preempt a running transition in exactly the same way.

The graph moves to kInTransition -> kAborting and requests the
stop token that was created when the transition started. Every
component dispatched by this transition carries that token.

From here no further component is dispatched: new components
are only taken from the transition while the graph is in
kInTransition.

While the graph is kAborting a result is only counted. The
transition is not advanced and nothing new is dispatched.
Every component in flight reports back. The longest a
cancellation can take is one ready timeout plus the
termination of the process that follows it.
With the last component in flight the graph moves to
kUndefinedState. Components that were already running are
deliberately left running.
handle the graph state
start the transition to the pending Run Target
set up a transition to the Run Target
The stop set of the new transition is derived from the live
state of the components, so everything the cancelled transition
left running is picked up and stopped if the new target does
not need it.
components ready to be stopped
A cancellation is observed at two points, each of which leaves the component
in a state the next transition can reason about:
1. Before the task is executed. A worker that picks up a task whose stop token
is already stopped does not run it and reports it as skipped. The component
keeps the state it had before the transition.
2. Between two startup attempts. The process of the failed attempt is already
gone; no further attempt is started, the component is deactivated and the
activation returns. The component is left stopped.
Nothing else is interrupted:
- The wait for a ready condition - the Running report, a configured file, or
the termination of the process itself - runs until the condition is
satisfied or the ready timeout expires. On the timeout the process that was
started is terminated with SIGTERM and, after the shutdown timeout, SIGKILL.
- A termination that has already been requested runs to its end. The process
may be writing its state to disk, so it always keeps its full shutdown
timeout before SIGKILL follows.
A component that reaches its ready condition despite the cancellation is
reported as activated and left running; the next transition stops it if its
target does not need it. The time a cancellation needs is therefore bounded by
the ready and shutdown timeouts of the components still in flight.
